rows.title: REFM Observer Program Database
rows.complete_abstract_element:
<abstract>The REFM Observer Program database consists of a suite of various data collected while deployed on board commercial fishing vessels or at shoreside processing plants participating in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska groundfish fisheries. These data have been collected from 1977 and they continue to date. While deployed at their assignments, observers collect data on the catch size, fishing locations, catch composition, length frequencies, age structures, marine mammal interactions, and a variety of special projects. The specific data components collected are outlined in the Groundfish Observer Manual. Once received by NMFS, these data are extensively checked for quality and are then entered onto an Oracle database and made available to authorized staff. 

Because the data are collected cooperatively from private commercial fishing interests, the data are protected from general release by confidentiality statutes. This protects the private business interests of industry while still providing NMFS the detailed information necessary to effectively manage. The staff authorized to use these data include NMFS scientists and managers participating in a broad range of activities including stock assessments, marine mammal interactions, food habits, fish age analyses, economic analyses, fishery management plan development, and in-season fishery management. The data are shared with other authorized users in the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) and North Pacific Fishery Management Council staff with similar responsibilities. 

Aggregations of observer data which protect confidentiality are periodically developed and released to the public. As well, observer data serve as essential building blocks for numerous public analyses, reports, and scientific documents.</abstract>
rows.purpose: To assist scientists and managers with fisheries management.

rows.title: Graphical Resource Database
rows.complete_abstract_element: <abstract>Database: Multi-Resources;  The Ship Escort/Response Vessel System (SERVS) of Alyeska Pipeline Service Company (Alyeska) is currently undertaking a major expansion and update of its environmental computer database for Prince William Sound and adjoining areas on the south-central coast of Alaska. The software, called the Graphical Resource Database (GRD), is part of Alyeska's commitment to the Prince William Sound Tanker Oil Discharge Prevention and Contingency Plan. The GRD consists of layers of coastal resource digital data records (such as seabird colony sites and sea otter concentration areas) that are linked to points, lines, or polygons depicting animal distributions on computer-generated maps. The expansion and update effort is coordinated by a committee consisting of representatives from federal and state natural resource trustee agencies, citizens oversight groups, Alyeska, and oil shipping companies. The data collection and checking process is conducted in accordance with written standard operating procedures. Data are gathered from the trustee agencies, compiled into Microsoft Excel spreadsheets, and verified using quality control/quality assurance procedures. The spreadsheets are then loaded into a commercially available mapping program, MapInfo , which serves as an intermediate graphical data management tool. The data are transferred from MapInfo to the GRD using FORTRAN programs. Data is available to federal and state agencies for oil spill planning and response.</abstract>
rows.purpose: Create a sensitive coastal resource database that will be held in common and mutually accessible by government trustee agencies and industry.

rows.title: Alaska Heritage Resources Survey
rows.complete_abstract_element: <abstract>Data Type: Cultural Resources;   The Alaska Heritage Resource Survey (AHRS) is an inventory of all reported historic and prehistoric sites within the State of Alaska and is maintained by the office of History and Archeology. This inventory of cultural resources includes objects, structures, buildings, sites, districts, and travel ways with a general provision that they be over 50 years old. To date nearly 15,000 sites have been recorded within Alaska (however, this is probably only a small percentage of the sites which may actually exist but are as yet unreported.) The fundamental use of the AHRS is to protect cultural resource sites from unwanted destruction. Various state, federal and private entities use the inventory for planning and reviewing development projects. The AHRS is primarily a map based system.</abstract>
